bio.en: Scott Wu is co-founder and CEO of Cognition, maker of Devin, the world's first autonomous AI software engineer that works like a remote engineer you collaborate with through Slack and a dedicated site.
bio.zh: Scott Wu 是 Cognition 的联合创始人兼 CEO，该公司打造了 Devin——全球首个自主式 AI 软件工程师，它像一个远程工程师，可通过 Slack 和专用网站与人协作。

summary.en: Scott explains how Devin evolved from a junior-engineer-level tool into a production system used by many companies, and what building and managing AI agents teaches us about the future of software. He shares Cognition's philosophy on autonomy, the human-in-the-loop workflows that work, and why agentic engineering is becoming a must-have skill. The episode is a front-row view of the autonomous-software-engineer frontier.
summary.zh: Scott 解释了 Devin 如何从一个“初级工程师水平”的工具，演进为被众多公司投入生产的系统，以及构建与管理 AI 智能体为我们揭示了软件未来的什么。他分享了 Cognition 关于自主性的理念、行之有效的“人在回路”工作流，以及为什么“智能体工程（agentic engineering）”正成为一项必备技能。本期是对“自主式 AI 软件工程师”前沿的前排透视。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Our whole team is only like 15 engineers a year. We use a ton of Devin when we're building Devin. Most folks on the team are definitely working with up to five Devins at once, and so Devin merges like several hundred pull requests into production in the Devin code bases every month.
turns.zh: 我们整个团队一年也就大概 15 个工程师。我们在构建 Devin 的时候用了大量的 Devin。团队里大多数人肯定同时在和最多五个 Devin 一起工作，所以 Devin 每个月往 Devin 的代码库里合并好几百个 pull request 到生产环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What percentage of your PRs are Devin versus humans right now?
turns.zh: 你现在有多少比例的 PR 是 Devin 而不是人类提交的？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: It's in the neighborhood of a quarter or so.
turns.zh: 大概在四分之一左右。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where do you think this will be at the end of the year?
turns.zh: 你觉得到年底这会到多少？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Honestly, we expect it to be a decent bit more than half.
turns.zh: 老实说，我们预期会略多于一半。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You guys are so ahead of how companies work with AI engineers.
turns.zh: 你们在公司和 AI 工程师协作的方式上，领先太多了。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: AI is going to be the biggest technology shift of our lives, so most of the big tech revolutions that we've had over the last 50 years, like personal computer, and the internet, and the mobile phone, they all had this big hardware component that was a big part of the distribution. Folks who were building for those industries kind of saw their market grow and grow and grow basically steadily year over year as the number of people with mobile phones increased, right, as the number of people connected to the internet increase. One of the things which is already I'd say different in AI, is just how explosive the technology can be. There's no weight on hardware distribution. It means that the space is just growing so exponentially.
turns.zh: AI 将是我们一生中最大的技术变革，所以过去 50 年里我们经历的那些大科技革命——比如个人电脑、互联网、手机——它们都有一个很大的硬件组成部分，那是它们分发的重要一环。为那些行业做开发的人，基本上随着拥有手机的人数增加、随着连上互联网的人数增加，看到他们的市场年复一年地稳步增长，对吧。我觉得 AI 已经不同的一个点，就是技术的爆发力可以有多强。它在硬件分发上没有重量。这意味着这个领域正在以指数级增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How is the act of being an engineer and building changing?
turns.zh: 作为工程师、以及"构建"这个行为，正在如何改变？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: I think there's going to be way more programmers and way more engineers a few years from now. Pretty quickly. The form factor of what it means to be a programmer obviously is going to change, but at the end of the day, of course the discipline is all about just being able to tell your computer what's do. And so in that lens, I really think that programming is only going to become more and more important as AI gets more powerful.
turns.zh: 我觉得几年后会有多得多的程序员、多得多的工程师。而且会很快。作为程序员意味着什么，它的形态显然会改变，但说到底，这个学科的本质就是能够告诉你的电脑该做什么。所以在那个视角下，我真的认为随着 AI 变得更强大，编程只会变得越来越重要。

turns.en: Hey Lenny. Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 嘿 Lenny。谢谢你邀请我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So integrations have become a big deal for AI products. Why is that?
turns.zh: 所以集成（integrations）对 AI 产品已经变得很重要了。为什么会这样？

turns.speaker: Brandon Foo
turns.en: Integrations are mission-critical for AI for two reasons. First, AI products need contacts from their customer's business data such as Google Drive files, Slack messages or CRM records. Second, for AI products to automate work on behalf of users, AI agents need to be able to take action across these different third-party tools.
turns.zh: 集成对 AI 来说是 mission-critical（至关重要的），有两个原因。第一，AI 产品需要来自客户业务数据的接触点，比如 Google Drive 文件、Slack 消息或 CRM 记录。第二，为了让 AI 产品能代表用户自动化工作，AI agent 需要能够在这些不同的第三方工具上采取行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So where does Paragon fit into all this?
turns.zh: 那么 Paragon 在所有这些里处于什么位置？

turns.speaker: Brandon Foo
turns.en: Well, these integrations are a pain to build and that's why Paragon provides an embedded platform that enables engineers to ship these product integrations in just days instead of months across every use case from RAG data ingestion to agentic actions.
turns.zh: 嗯，这些集成做起来很痛苦，所以 Paragon 提供了一个嵌入式平台，让工程师能在几天而不是几个月内部署这些产品集成，覆盖从 RAG 数据摄取到 agentic actions（智能体动作）的所有用例。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I know from firsthand experience that maintenance is even harder than just building it for the first time.
turns.zh: 而且我根据 firsthand 经验知道，维护比第一次把它建出来还要难。

turns.en: Exactly. We believe product teams should focus engineering efforts and competitive advantages, not integrations. That's why companies like You.com, AI21 and hundreds of others use Paragon to accelerate their integration strategy.
turns.zh: 没错。我们相信产品团队应该把工程精力放在竞争优势上，而不是集成上。这就是为什么像 You.com、AI21 以及数百家其他公司用 Paragon 来加速他们的集成战略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you want to avoid wasting months of engineering on integrations that your customers need, check out paragon@useparagon.com/lenny. Scott, thank you so much for being here and welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 如果你想避免在你的客户需要的集成上浪费几个月的工程时间，去看看 paragon@useparagon.com/lenny。Scott，非常感谢你能来，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Thanks so much for having me. Excited to be on.
turns.zh: 太感谢你邀请我了。很高兴上节目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm really excited to have you here because you are building and you've been building something that is very different from what a lot of other AI companies have been doing for a long time, although they are starting to converge to where you guys are now. We're going to talk about that and it's also just such a unique point in the history of AI and just the journey of AI. And so it's really cool to be chatting right now. And I feel like we're going to chat again in a few years and be like, wow, we were so right about so much and so wrong about so much.
turns.zh: 我真的很兴奋你能来，因为你在做的、而且已经做了一段时间的这件事，和很多其他 AI 公司长期以来做的非常不同，虽然它们现在开始收敛到你们所在的位置了。我们要聊那个，而且这也正好是 AI 历史和 AI 旅程一个非常独特的时点。所以现在聊真的很酷。而且我觉得几年后我们会再聊一次，然后会想，哇，我们对了这么多、也错了这么多。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so I'm excited to have you here. Let's start with talking about Devin, giving people an understanding of just what the heck Devin is, is the main product that you guys build. What is the simplest way to understand what is Devin?
turns.zh: 所以我兴奋你能来。我们先从聊 Devin 开始，让人们理解 Devin 到底是个什么鬼，也就是你们做的主要产品。理解 Devin 最简单的方式是什么？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Absolutely. And so Devin is a fully autonomous software engineer that is going to work on tasks end to end, and so there are a lot of great tools for all parts of the stack of the AI code workflow. What Devin does is it is a full asynchronous workflow, and so you can tag Devin on an issue in Slack, you're talking about an issue and you tag Devin, you can tag Devin in Linear, you can have Devin and Devin will make pull requests in your GitHub, and so it's very much built to work with engineering teams as your junior engineer.
turns.zh: 当然。Devin 是一个完全自主的软件工程师，会端到端地做任务，所以在 AI 代码工作流的技术栈各个部分都有很多很棒的工具。Devin 做的是一套完整的异步工作流，所以你可以在 Slack 的一个 issue 上 @ Devin，你正聊着一个 issue 然后你 @ Devin，你可以在 Linear 里 @ Devin，你可以让 Devin，然后 Devin 会在你的 GitHub 里建 pull request，所以它被构建得非常适合作为你的初级工程师和工程团队一起工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing, okay. So I remember when you guys launched this, there was this big pitch of this is your new AI engineer and it was really good at a lot of stuff. It wasn't great at other things. It's been a year now about since you guys launched, is that right?
turns.zh: 太棒了，好。所以我还记得你们发布它的时候，有一个很大的 pitch，说这是你的新 AI 工程师，它在很多事情上真的很好。其他一些事情上不怎么行。现在大约一年了，是吧？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 对，对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the best way to think about the level of seniority that engineer had back in the day when you guys launched and then the level of seniority of engineer today if that's, I don't know, measure of how to think about Devin?
turns.zh: 最能让人理解你们发布时那个工程师的资深度、以及今天这个工程师的资深度的方式是什么——如果那是，我不知道，一个衡量怎么思考 Devin 的指标的话？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah, and it's crazy to think about by the way, because a year ago when we did the initial launch, I mean people didn't really believe that an agent was possible. Right. And it was, I mean, it was a very different time. So like start of 2024, things with model capabilities were definitely quite a bit earlier on, reasoning especially was quite a bit earlier on. And yeah, I mean, in the time since then it's obviously developed a lot. I think in terms of practical skills, there's some comparisons we make. Sometimes we kind of say, well, when we got started it was kind of like a high school CS student and then as time went on, it became more of a college intern and now it's like a junior engineer. But I would say though that those are more rough guidelines because I really like the phrase jagged intelligence for example, because obviously there are certain things that it is much better at than a human. There are certain things that it's much worse at than a human. (00:07:52): And I think over the last year we've learned a lot especially about not just coding agents but agents in general just really building out how all of us should be working and interacting with agents as part of our flow. And so a lot of the things that we built, I mean, there was no Slack, there was no GitHub integration, there was no Linear, there was no interactive planning phase working back and forth. There was no way to touch up Devin's code. And so a lot of the features that we've built on the product side since then have really been about basically yeah, figuring out how to make working with Devin and handing off tasks to Devin as smooth of an experience as possible.
turns.zh: 是的，而且顺便说这想想就很疯狂，因为一年前我们做最初发布时，我的意思是人们真的不相信一个 agent 是可能的。对吧。而且，我的意思是，那是一个非常不同的时期。所以 2024 年初，模型能力肯定还早得多，尤其是推理能力还早得多。而且是的，我的意思是，从那以后它显然发展了很多。我觉得就实际技能而言，我们做一些比较。有时候我们 kinda 说，嗯，我们刚开始时它有点像一个高中 CS 学生，然后随着时间推移，它变得更像一个大学实习生，现在它就像一个初级工程师。但我会说那些更多是粗略的指引，因为我真的很喜欢"jagged intelligence"（锯齿状智能）这个短语，因为显然有些事情它比人类好得多。有些事情它比人类差得多。(00:07:52)：而且我觉得过去这一年我们学到了很多，尤其是不仅关于编码 agent，而是关于 agent 整体——真的在构建我们所有人应该怎么作为工作流的一部分和 agent 一起工作、互动。所以我们建的很多东西，我的意思是，那时候没有 Slack、没有 GitHub 集成、没有 Linear、没有来回互动的规划阶段。也没有办法去润色 Devin 的代码。所以从那以后我们在产品端建的大量功能，真的就是关于，是的，搞清楚怎么让和 Devin 一起工作、把任务交给 Devin 变成尽可能顺滑的体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so interesting. So a lot of the work has gone not into how do we just make Devin the best possible engineer, but it's how to work with this new type of entity that we haven't ever worked with.
turns.zh: 那太有意思了。所以很多工作不是投在"我们怎么把 Devin 做成尽可能好的工程师"，而是"怎么和这种我们从未共事过的新类型实体一起工作"。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: I think it's a 50/50 of both. I think the capabilities obviously have improved a ton and we've seen these get better and get measurably better. But I think the other side of it is everything to do with yeah, really the product interface and the tools and so on. And I think today folks generally know how to use chatbots and to with chatbots, right, and that's an interface that people are familiar with and obviously with agents it's still like a real curve, I think to learn how to use them and how to get the most out of them. And so it's really exciting to see a lot of others starting to build and do a lot more in the agent space as well. But I think this is the kind of thing that we're all really figuring out together as a space.
turns.zh: 我觉得这两者是五五开。我觉得能力显然提升了一大截，我们看到它们变得更好、而且是可衡量地更好。但我觉得另一面是和产品的界面、工具等等相关的一切。而且我觉得今天人们普遍知道怎么用聊天机器人、和聊天机器人一起用，对吧，那是一个人们熟悉的界面，而显然和 agent 一起用，我觉得还是有一个真正的学习曲线，去学会怎么用它们、怎么最大化从它们身上得到的东西。所以看到很多其他人也开始在 agent 领域构建、做更多，真的很令人兴奋。但我觉得这类事情是我们作为一个领域真的在一起共同摸索的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What can you share about just the scale of Devin at this point, whatever you're comfortable sharing, and then just where do you think the level of Devin's coding abilities will be in a year?
turns.zh: 关于 Devin 目前的规模，你能分享什么——任何你愿意分享的——然后就是你觉得一年里 Devin 的编码能力会到什么水平？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: So we work with companies of all stages and sizes. On the smallest end, it goes to startups of just one or two people who are using Devin to build out a lot of their kind of initial prototype or initial product all the way up to big public companies, Fortune 100 companies or public banks or things like that who are using Devin across their engineering teams. In general, we've seen a huge range of the use cases there. And obviously the kinds of engineering work that you're doing at a one or two person startup, they're very different from the kind of work that you're doing at a public bank. (00:09:55): But throughout it's all been basically yeah, being that junior buddy of yours that makes you go faster and really multiplies you, I would say. I think it can multiply you as an engineer obviously by just letting you work with your own team of Devins instead of having to be kind of fully synchronous on a single task. And then it's also kind of multiplying your team and multiplying your team's knowledge base because Devin really accumulates a lot of the knowledge from working with every member of your team and is able to bring that into each new session.
turns.zh: 所以我们和所有阶段、所有规模的公司合作。最小的一端，是只有一两个人的初创公司，用 Devin 来构建他们大量的初始原型或初始产品，一直到大型上市公司、财富 100 强公司或上市银行之类的，它们在自己的工程团队里用 Devin。总的来说，我们看到那边的用例范围非常广。而且显然你在一两个人的初创公司里做的工程工作，和你在一家上市银行里做的那种工作非常不同。(00:09:55)：但贯穿始终的，基本上就是，是的，做你那个让你走得更快、真正放大你的初级伙伴。我觉得它显然能通过让你和自己的 Devin 团队合作、而不必在同一个任务上完全同步，来放大你作为一个工程师。而且它也在放大你的团队、放大你团队的知识库，因为 Devin 真的会从和你团队每个成员的合作中积累大量知识，并能够把它带进每一场新会话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We're going to show people how it actually works later in the podcast. We're going to do a few live demos, but let's actually go to the beginning of the journey. What's just the origin story of Devin? How did this all begin?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们稍后会在播客里给大家展示它实际是怎么工作的。我们会做几个现场 demo，但我们先回到这段旅程的开头。Devin 的起源故事是什么？这一切是怎么开始的？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: The founding team, I mean most of us have known each other for years and years and years actually. And for almost everyone, this is our first time working together, but we've known each other a long time. And we all actually had our own kind of journeys in AI for the last decade or so. And so for myself, I ran a company before this called Lunchclub, which was an AI for a professional networking product and I ran that for about five years. And one of my co-founders, Steven was one of the first engineers at a company called Scale AI, which has obviously grown a lot and done very well. My other co-founder Walden, was an early engineer at a company called Cursor, which has also obviously grown a lot and done really well. And our whole team was kind of like that. Many of us knew each other from competitive programming and math competitions, but we had stayed very closely in touch in the decade since then and we've all kind of all had our own journeys. (00:11:22): And so we had one person who was running teams at Neuro, we had one person who was at Waymo, someone who had their own YC tools startup for machine learning, and we were really excited to build something together. And this was around late 2023, so about a year and a half ago at this point. And yeah, when we got started, I mean I think there were a couple of things that we felt really strongly about and one was that reinforcement learning was really working and was going to be the next big paradigm shift in capabilities. Back then it was the initial ChatGPT launch in 2022, and those models were, to first order were what we would call imitation learning in AI, right, which is basically you have the model read all the texts that you can find on the internet and then train it to talk like somebody on the internet would talk. Right. And there are kind of obviously a lot more details on top of that, but that's kind of the first order pass of what was really done. (00:12:16): And it was amazing. Right. I mean, it passed the churn test, it was able to respond and to have encyclopedic knowledge about a lot of things. And I think this new paradigm which we've gotten into over this last year or year and a half is really high compute RL, which is a very different paradigm, right, which is basically the ability to go and do work on task and put something together and then be evaluated on whether that was correct or incorrect and use that knowledge to decide what to do and to learn from that. Right. And so we felt very strongly that that was going to happen. I think for us, code was the natural thing to work on for a couple reasons. One, because we're all programmer nerds ourselves, and so teaching AI to code is about as cool as it gets for us, but also because code has this whole automated feedback loop, right, where you can run the code and that is the kind of automated feedback that really feeds into the RL, which makes these models so great at coding. (00:13:06): And then the other thing that we felt very strongly about was that the product experience was going to shift from what I'll call text completion to agents basically. Right. And to first order, I would kind of say there's been a lot of great experiences in text completion. It's been used for marketing, it's been used for customer support, it's been used for education and in Coda obviously as well. The GitHub copilot was kind of really the dominant product of that initial wave. Right. (00:13:34): But I think that the big shift that we really felt we would see is moving from kind of this text to text model to an actual autonomous system that can make decisions, that can interact with the real world, that can take in feedback, that can iterate and take multiple steps to solve problems. And now we call that agents, but that was what we were really excited about at the time. So it was always coding, it was always agents. And in some ways that kind of feels like it should have been cleared from the start. But even with that, I feel like we've pivoted eight times or something within coding agents over the last year and a half, so.
turns.zh: 创始团队，我的意思是，我们大多数人其实已经互相认识了好多年好多年。而且对几乎所有人来说，这是我们第一次一起工作，但我们认识很久了。而且我们其实在过去十年左右都在 AI 上各自有自己的旅程。就我自己而言，我在这之前运营过一家公司叫 Lunchclub，是一个职业社交的 AI 产品，我运营了大约五年。我的一个联合创始人 Steven 是 Scale AI 最早的一批工程师之一，那家公司显然成长了很多、做得很好。我的另一个联合创始人 Walden，是 Cursor 这家公司的早期工程师，那家公司也显然成长了很多、做得真的很好。我们整个团队都差不多是这样。我们很多人是从竞赛编程和数学竞赛认识的，但在那之后的十年里我们一直保持紧密联系，而且我们都各自有自己的旅程。(00:11:22)：所以我们有个人在 Neuro 带团队，有个人在 Waymo，有人有自己的 YC 机器学习工具初创公司，我们真的很兴奋能一起做点东西。那是 2023 年底左右，所以到目前为止大概一年半前。而且是的，我们开始时，我的意思是，我觉得有几件事我们真的非常笃定，其中一件是强化学习真的在起作用，而且会成为下一个能力上的范式转变。那时候是 2022 年最初的 ChatGPT 发布，那些模型粗略地说就是我们所谓的 AI 里的模仿学习，对吧，基本就是你让模型读所有能在网上找到的文本，然后训练它像网上的某个人那样说话。对。上面显然还有更多细节，但那大致就是真正做了什么的一阶描述。(00:12:16)：而且它很惊人。对。我的意思是……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah, and there's even, I mean OpenAI, ChatGPT, Anthropic and Claude and Google. Yeah, it's funny. Yeah, yeah, I agree. So when we got started, it wasn't even really a company. I mean, it was more like a project or a hackathon almost. We got a bunch, we booked an Airbnb basically for a couple of weeks. This was around Thanksgiving time and just got a bunch of people together who were just excited to hack on some projects and build something cool. And it's funny, actually the first thing that we were building for actually was more solving these more contest programming problems and using an agentic loop to really do better on that. And so obviously if you run your code on the test cases, you can evaluate, there's a lot of agentic work that you can do there to try and do better, and that we spent some time on that initially. And then we've kind of gone from, I mean the story of the whole company for us in some sense has been going from hacker house to hacker house. (00:15:26): So after that we had another hacker house and that's where kind of some of the initial ideas for Devin came and really building a software engineering agent and not just a coding agent and having to interact with a lot of these tools, but even then there were so many iterations. (00:16:11): And so it's yeah, it's been a fun journey. turns.zh: 是的，而且甚至，我的意思是 OpenAI、ChatGPT、Anthropic 和 Claude、还有 Google。是的，很好笑。是的，是的，我同意。所以我们开始时，它甚至真的不是一个公司。我的意思是，它更像是一个项目或者差不多一个 hackathon（黑客松）。我们订了一个 Airbnb，基本上住了几个星期。那是感恩节前后，就是把一群只是兴奋来 hack 一些项目、做点酷东西的人聚在一起。而且很好笑，实际上我们最初要做的更多是解决那些竞赛编程问题，用一个 agentic loop（智能体循环）真的在那上面做得更好。所以显然如果你在测试用例上跑你的代码，你可以评估，那里有很多 agentic 工作你可以做来试图做得更好，我们最初在那上面花了一些时间。然后我们 kinda 从——我在某种意义上整个公司的故事对我们来说就是从 hacker house（黑客屋）到 hacker house。(00:15:26)：所以在那之后我们有了另一个 hacker house，那里就是 Devin 一些最初想法的来源，以及真的去构建一个软件工程 agent 而不只是一个编码 agent，并且得和很多这些工具互动，但即便如此还有那么多迭代。甚至比如和 Devin 对话这个想法，是我们得想出来的。对。最初，就只是你交出一个任务然后它工作、然后它给你看这一整块完成的代码。对。而现在显然就像你可以在任何时候跳进去，你可以对计划给反馈，你们可以在和 Devin 工作时一起把任务的范围敲定。很多这些东西我们显然得开发出来，而且我们当然对用例、形态学了很多。我们在能力上、以及 Devin 使用工具、debug、做决策的能力上，做了很多大的改进和阶跃式的改进。(00:16:11)：所以是的，它一直是……[truncated]

turns.zh: 是的，所以我们是 2023 年 11 月开始的，那基本上就是 hackathon 模式。我们在 2024 年初正式成了一家公司，然后我们最初发布是在 3 月。所以那是停不下来的，我的意思是过去 17 个月一直没停过，但走到发布，然后显然和企业合作、更多地开发产品、把它建好并让它适用于很多实际用例，然后在去年 12 月让它完全自助可用。而且我们现在显然几周前刚推出了 2.0。所以对我们来说一直是非常忙碌的时期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Understatement of the century. Let me ask this question because you touched on it a bit, this whole idea of Devin as a person and this idea of creating a personality for Devin. It's unlike any other, I believe, AI app. No one else has a name and you don't think of it as a person. What made you guys decide to go that approach and just how do you design it to work well that way?
turns.zh: 世纪之轻描淡写。让我问这个问题，因为你稍微提到了，就是 Devin 作为一个"人"的整个想法，以及给 Devin 创造一个人格的这个想法。我相信这和其他任何 AI 应用都不同。没人有名字，你也不把它当人想。是什么让你们决定走那条路，以及你们怎么设计它让它那样很好地工作？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: I would say it's a decision we're pretty proud of, I would say. I mean, I think there's a lot of different product experiences out there, and I think the thing that really makes Devin unique in what it does is that you can really hand off and more and more what we've seen honestly is that I think a lot of kind of explaining the Devin experience to folks is really just explain it as, yeah, this is your junior buddy. And that goes for a lot of the parts of the flow where in the onboarding for example, initially I would say we've definitely had a lot of users come in and just kind of see the blank screen and not really know, or they'd ask, "Hey, I'm going to do this whole big re-architecture, the whole code base." (00:18:21): And basically what we've learned over time is to basically get folks to think more like whoa, whoa, whoa, let's work on getting the repository set up first. Let's make sure we hand Devin a couple one pointer tasks so it can get familiar with the code base. Let's get it the thing. If Devin needs to be able to test the code or run the linter or CI or things like that. Obviously we want to make sure Devin's got its own virtual machine set up to be able to do that. (00:18:45): And similarly, I think the usage pattern, I think often it wasn't clear and obviously you can sit and just kind of watch Devin do it action by action and work that way, but we found that the best workflow really as a team building a lot of stuff was to work with multiple Devins and to run them asynchronously and to kick them off and to only jump in basically as you needed to provide feedback or steer the plan or anything like that. And so in many ways, I think Devin as a name really is our attempt to kind of capture the soul of that as a product where it really is treating it like a bit more of an autonomous entity that you can hand off tasks, that you can work with, that you should be teaching and learning with over time.
turns.zh: 我会说这是一个我们相当自豪的决定，我会说。我的意思是，我觉得外面有很多不同的产品体验，而我觉得真正让 Devin 在它做的事上独特的地方，是你真的可以把手头的任务交出去，而且我们越来越看到的，老实说，很多向人们解释 Devin 体验的方式真的就是把它解释成，是的，这是你的初级伙伴。这在流程的很多部分都适用，比如在 onboarding（上手）时，起初我得说我们确实有很多用户进来，就看着那个空白屏幕、不太知道，或者他们会问"嘿，我要做这一整个大的重构，整个代码库。"(00:18:21)：而基本上我们随着时间学到的，是让人们对，哇哇哇，先让我们把仓库设置好。让我们确保我们交给 Devin 几个 one pointer 任务，这样它能熟悉代码库。让我们把它搞定。如果 Devin 需要能测试代码、或者跑 linter 或者 CI 或者这类东西。显然我们想确保 Devin 有自己的虚拟机设置好，能够做那个。(00:18:45)：类似地，我觉得使用模式，我觉得经常它并不清晰，而且显然你可以坐着、就看着 Devin 一个动作一个动作地做、那样工作，但我们发现最好的工作流真的作为一个团队构建很多东西，是和多个 Devin 一起工作、异步地跑它们、启动它们，并且基本上只在你需要提供反馈、或者给计划掌舵、或者任何类似事情时才跳进去。所以在很多方面，我觉得 Devin 作为一个名字，真的是我们试图捕捉那个作为一个产品的灵魂——它真的把它当作一个更自主的实体，你可以交任务给它、你可以和它一起工作、你应该随着时间教它、和它一起学习。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: By the way, we're all software engineers ourselves. It's like I'm a programmer by training and still a programmer at heart certainly. And I think the way that we've always thought about it is there's layers of abstraction and there's tools, and one way I would say it at a high level is kind of I think of AI in general as, yeah, I mean computers are obviously getting more and more intelligence and are able to do more and more and it's possible there may come a day where computers truly do everything that we do and humans are not responsible for any of it. (00:20:20): I don't expect that to come particularly soon, but I guess what I would say is until that point, for as long as we're still part of the equation, one of the most important things to do obviously is for us as humans is to instruct our computers on what we want and what we want to build and what we want to do. Right. And software engineering is, we think of it today obviously as Python and C++ and JavaScript and all these things, but at the end of the day, of course the discipline is all about just being to tell your computer what to do. And so in that lens, I really think that programming is, if anything, is only going to become more and more important as AI gets more powerful. And I think the thing that's really exciting for us is yeah, it's really seeing that kind of iterative transformation. And so you ask what things look like today, and I would say, yeah, it really is like having a junior buddy or really a team of junior buddies that you can work with. Right. (00:21:12): And so every engineer on our team, we use a ton of Devin when we're building Devin, and so Devin merges several hundred pull requests into production in the Devin code bases every month, which is, I mean, our whole team is only 15 engineers, and so it's a pretty sizable fraction of all the code that we write. And the way that we use it is basically, yeah, everyone's got their whole team of Devins. If you're going to be looking through various issues, if you're going through feature requests, if you're going through bugs, if you're going through new paradigms that you want to build, then it is naturally the case that there's a lot of handoff points where you just say, "Hey, at Devin, here's what's going on. Can you please take a pass at this?" Right. (00:21:47): And sometimes Devin will be able to do the task 100% autonomously and just makes the PR and then you merge the PR and that's great. Sometimes you want to be able to jump in for the 10 or 20% that really needs your help. Maybe there's a few details with how exactly you want to scope it or how you're architecting this feature, or maybe you want to go and test the front end at the end yourself to make sure it looks exactly the way that you want and give your one or two lines of feedback after that. Right. But a lot of it is really yeah, is kind of like yeah, learning to work with Devin to be able to just do more in parallel and build more.
turns.zh: 顺便说，我们自己都是软件工程师。我训练上是程序员，而且心里当然还是个程序员。我觉得我们一直思考它的方式是，有抽象层、有工具，而我在一个高层次上会说的一种方式就是，我觉得总体上把 AI 想成，是的，我的意思是电脑显然在变得越来越智能、能做越来越多，而且有可能有一天电脑真的会做我们做的所有事、人类不用再对任何事负责。(00:20:20)：我不期待那个特别快到来，但我想说的是，在那之前，只要我们还是这个等式的一部分，显然最重要的事情之一，就是我们作为人类去指示我们的电脑我们想要什么、想构建什么、想做什么。对。而软件工程，我们今天当然把它想成 Python、C++、JavaScript 和所有这些东西，但说到底，这个学科的本质当然就是告诉你的电脑该做什么。所以在那个视角下，我真的认为编程如果有什么的话，只会随着 AI 更强大而变得越来越重要。而且我觉得对我们来说真正令人兴奋的是，是的，真的看到那种迭代式的转变。所以你问今天事情是什么样子，我会说，是的，它真的就像有了一个初级伙伴、或者真的是一队初级伙伴你可以一起工作。对。(00:21:12)：所以我们团队的每个工程师，我们在构建 Devin 的时候用了大量的 Devin，所以 Devin 每个月往 Devin 的代码库里合并好几百个 pull request，这，我的意思是，我们整个团队只有 15 个工程师，所以它占我们写的所有代码相当大的一部分。而我们用的方式基本就是，是的，每个人都有自己的一整队 Devin。如果你要去看……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: ... about defining the problem that you're facing and really thinking through exactly what is the solution that you want to build. Thinking through the architecture, thinking through the details, and really mapping out in your mind exactly what you want to build basically and what you want to have your computer do. I think that's what makes software engineering really great and I think that's the funnest part of software engineering. (00:24:21): I think, at the same time, that's probably in the neighborhood of 10% of the average software engineer's time, right? Because 90% of the time is you've got this Kubernetes error, then you've got to debug, and you have to see what went wrong and the system crash, or you left some port open and this is messing up, or there's a bug report that you have to take care of, or you've got to migrate your code, or you got it upgraded to a new version or things like that. A lot more implementation. (00:24:48): One of the ways that we've kind of thought about Devin in building Devin is really allowing engineers to go from bricklayer to architect, so to speak. A lot of it is just getting to the point where you can do the high-level directing and you can basically specify things exactly how you want. I think it's very much about still having the human in control and having the human able to do the full specification, but just multiplying the magnitude of what you can do and what you can build in one day or one hour or however long.
turns.zh: ……关于定义你面对的问题、并且真正想清楚你到底想构建的是什么解决方案。想清楚架构，想清楚细节，并且在你脑中真正描绘出你想构建的、以及你想让你的电脑做的到底是什么。我觉得那就是让软件工程真的很棒的东西，而且我觉得那是软件工程最有趣的部分。(00:24:21)：同时，我觉得那大概平均软件工程师时间的 10% 左右，对吧？因为 90% 的时间是你有个 Kubernetes 错误，然后你得 debug，你得看什么地方出错了、系统崩了，或者你留了个端口开着把这搞乱了，或者有个 bug 报告你得处理，或者你得迁移你的代码，或者你把它升级到新版本之类的。多得多的是实现。(00:24:48)：我们在构建 Devin 时思考 Devin 的一种方式，就是真的让工程师从砌砖工变成架构师，可以说。很多就是到达那个点：你能做高层的指挥、你能基本按你想要的方式精确指定东西。我觉得它很大程度上仍然是关于让人保持掌控、让人能做完整的规格说明，只是放大你在一天、一小时或不管多久里能做的事和能构建的东西的幅度。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the future, say someone is trying to get into software engineering, thinking about becoming an engineer, first of all, do you think people should... Classic question everyone's getting these days. Should you still learn to code?
turns.zh: 未来，假设有人想进入软件工程、想着成为工程师，首先，你觉得人们应不应该……这是最近每个人都常被问的经典问题。你还应该学编程吗？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love your perspective there. And then two, for people that are engineers today, what skills do you think will be more and more important and then less important in this discussion of moving from bricklayer to architect?
turns.zh: 我很想听你那个角度的看法。然后第二，对今天已经是工程师的人，你觉得哪些技能会越来越重要、哪些在这个从砌砖工到架构师的讨论里会越来越不重要？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah, for sure. I love this question. First of all, the question of whether you should still learn to code, my answer would be absolutely yes. I think, to a large extent, when you take computer science classes and when you learn these fundamentals, sure you're learning a little bit about how a particular language is, syntax works or something like that. But honestly, most of what you're learning really is about the ability to logically break down problems for number one. And two, I would say is just the model of a computer and a lot of these decisions and a lot of the abstractions that we've built over time. (00:26:11): What is a database and how should you think about a database? What is a garbage collection system and how do those work and all of these different pieces? The reason I think that's important is because it's the same with a lot of these other... Arguably we've already gone through these phases in programming and I think this next one is going to be somewhat faster and somewhat bigger, but in many ways a similar flavor, which is when you work with Python today, obviously, a lot of things are already abstracted away from you. (00:26:38): In some sense, someone from 50 years ago might already call Python. You just get to explain in English what you want and now the computer does it for you. That's great and I think it's really powerful. It's opened it up. I mean, we have far more programmers, obviously, than we ever have before because of that, but I would say certainly as you're building your skills as an engineer, it really helps a lot to understand the abstractions and to be able to peel the layers beneath. Folks will use assembly for example if they're really performance optimizing a piece of code, but also in order to build good systems and to understand these things, you certainly want to understand these abstractions of how does networking work. (00:27:18): What is TCP/IP like exactly or what happens with this Python code when it gets interpreted or all of these details. Similarly, I think we will get to a state where, with no experience at all, you're going to be able to build some pretty cool stuff and to do some pretty amazing work just by explaining what it is that you want. But I think that, for quite some time, you really want to be able to think precisely about the details, to peel back the abstractions, to be very precise about what it is that you want to build and how.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。我爱这个问题。首先，该不该还学编程，我的答案是绝对要。我觉得很大程度上，当你上计算机科学课、当你学这些基础时，当然你是在学一点某种特定语言的语法怎么运作之类的。但老实说，你学的绝大部分真的是关于第一，把问题逻辑性地拆解开的能力。第二，我会说是电脑的模型，以及我们随着时间建起来的很多这些决策和抽象。(00:26:11)：什么是数据库、你应该怎么思考数据库？什么是垃圾回收系统、它们怎么运作、以及所有这些不同的部分？我觉得那重要的原因是，它和很多其他这些……可以说我们已经经历过编程的这些阶段了，而且我觉得下一个会稍微快一点、稍微大一点，但在很多方面是类似的味道，也就是今天你用 Python 工作时，显然很多东西已经被从你这里抽象掉了。(00:26:38)：在某种意义上有个从 50 年前的人可能就已经会叫 Python。你只要用英语解释你想要什么，然后电脑就替你做了。那很棒，而且我觉得它真的强大。它把它打开了。我的意思是，正因如此，我们显然比以往有远多得多的程序员，但我会说，当然在你作为工程师构建技能时，理解这些抽象、并且能够剥开底下的层，真的很有帮助。比如人们在极度性能优化一段代码时会用汇编，但也为了构建好系统、理解这些东西，你当然想理解这些抽象——网络是怎么运作的。(00:27:18)：TCP/IP 到底是什么样的、或者当这段 Python 代码进入……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then for skills that you think are more and more valuable for engineers, where should engineers today be leaning more and more into versus like, "Forget this. I don't need to think about this anymore"?
turns.zh: 然后对于那些你觉得对工程师越来越有价值的技能，今天的工程师应该越来越多地 lean into 什么，对比"忘了这个吧，我不用再想这个了"？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: For sure. I think architect... I mean, we already have a term for architect and engineering and I think it is directionally the right term. It's, I think, one thing to just do a routine implementation and write boilerplate code and things like that. I would say that, in many ways, AI coding has already made us much faster at that, but I think a lot of the core questions of understanding very complex systems and working in the context of the whole company and thinking about the product that you're building or the work that you're doing and understanding, "Okay, what are the problems that we want to solve? How do we want to solve those problems? What is exactly the solution that we want to build? What are all of these key decisions and trade-offs that we're going to be making?" (00:28:40): Basically, I think folks who are able to do that really, really well are just going to be able to leverage themselves more and more. If anything, I think there's going to be way more programmers and way more engineers a few years from now than there are today. I think pretty quickly the form factor of what it means to be a programmer, obviously, is going to change. And in some sense, it already has, but I think there's just going to be so much more for us to build. Folks talk about Jevons Paradox all the time. I mean, software is truly the shining example of Jevons Paradox, where we have always managed as a society to find more and more things that we want to build software for and build more code for. I really think there's a lot more out there to do.
turns.zh: 当然。我觉得架构……我的意思是，我们已经有"架构师"这个工程和术语了，而且我觉得方向上是那个对的词。做常规的实现、写样板代码之类的，我会说在很多方面 AI 编码已经让我们在那上面快多了，但我觉得很多核心问题——理解非常复杂的系统、在整个公司的情境里工作、思考你构建的产品或你做的工作、理解"好，我们想解决什么问题？我们想怎么解决那些问题？我们到底想构建的解决方案是什么？我们要做的所有那些关键决策和权衡是什么？"(00:28:40)：基本上，我觉得能真的、真的把那些做得很好的人，就只是能越来越放大自己。如果有什么的话，我觉得几年后会有比今天多得多的程序员、多得多的工程师。我觉得很快，作为程序员意味着什么的形态显然会改变。而且在某种意义上有已经改变了，但我觉得会有太多太多我们要构建的东西。人们一直在谈 Jevons Paradox（杰文斯悖论）。我的意思是，软件真的是 Jevons Paradox 的闪亮例子，我们作为一个社会总是能找到越来越多我们想为它构建软件、构建更多代码的东西。我真的觉得外面还有好多要做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For people that don't know Jevons Paradox, can you briefly explain it?
turns.zh: 对不知道 Jevons Paradox 的人，你能简单解释一下吗？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Absolutely. Yeah. Jevons Paradox just says that as the price of something goes down, it can still be the case that the total spend on it actually goes up. You can think about this with money, you can think about this with time or resources, but the direct version here is, I think, as it becomes easier and easier to program and as programming becomes more and more effective, I think we're going to have a lot more programmers. I think in a kind of zero-sum view, you might say, "Well, we're going to be 10 times faster at software engineering and it means that we're going to need 10 times fewer software engineers." But I think in practice, what really is going to happen is actually we're going to build even more than 10 times as much code. And because all of the work that we do is so capped, obviously, on our ability to actually build and execute and iterate, we're going to have so many great ideas out there, we're going to have so many great products out there. People are going to build a lot more personalized experiences, for example, and there's going to be a lot to do.
turns.zh: 当然。是的。Jevons Paradox 就是说，随着某样东西的价格下降，总花费反而仍然可能上升。你可以用钱来想，你可以用时间或资源来想，但这里直接的版本是，我觉得，随着编程变得越来越容易、随着编程变得越来越有效，我们会有多得多的程序员。在一种零和的观点里，你可能会说"好吧，我们在软件工程上会快 10 倍，意味着我们需要的软件工程师会少 10 倍。"但我觉得实际上会发生的是，我们会构建比 10 倍还多的代码。而且因为我们做的所有工作都明显受限于我们实际去构建、执行、迭代的能力，外面会有那么多好点子、那么多好产品。比如人们会构建多得多个性化的体验，而且会有好多要做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going back to the way you guys use Devin, you said that every engineer has this fleet of Devins. How many Devins per engineer do you find most people are working with these days at your company?
turns.zh: 回到你们用 Devin 的方式，你说每个工程师都有这支 Devin 舰队。你们公司里现在大多数人同时和多少个 Devin 工作？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah. It's very asynchronous. Obviously, you can kick them up and start them up and shut them down basically as you see fit, but most folks on the team are often working with up to five Devins at once, I would say. It's a nice flow where you think through, "All right, what are the five things that we want to get done today?" You have Devin one do number one, you have Devin two do number two, Devin three... For what it's worth, I think it's taken us some time to adjust to it and get to the point where it's really intuitive for us, but I think it's definitely a different experience where you're handing off most things asynchronously. (00:31:14): The goal for each of your tasks is to be there for the parts that really need your expertise, either you really, really need to define exactly what it is that you're solving for and what you're building or maybe some of the more complex parts where you want to steer Devin towards, particularly what kinds of changes you want to make. "I want the class to be set up this way and we should go and change all the downstream references to this as well or whatever." But basically having Devin do the bulk of the work asynchronously with you.
turns.zh: 是的。它非常异步。显然，你可以启动它们、开始它们、基本按需关掉它们，但团队里大多数人我经常说同时在和多达五个 Devin 一起工作。这是一个很好的流：你想清楚"好，我们今天想搞定哪五件事？"你让 Devin 一做第一件，Devin 二做第二件，Devin 三……说实话，我觉得我们花了一些时间才适应它、到达它对我们真的直观的那个点，但我觉得它绝对是一种不同的体验，你大部分东西是异步交出去的。(00:31:14)：你每个任务的目标，是在那些真的需要你专业知识的环节在场——要么你真的、真的需要精确定义你正在解决的是什么、你在构建什么，要么也许一些更复杂的部分你想把 Devin 引向，特别是你想做哪些改动。"我想让这个类这样设置，而且我们也应该去改所有对它的下游引用什么的。"但基本就是让 Devin 异步地做大部分工作，和你一起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then how many engineers do you guys have roughly?
turns.zh: 那你们大概有多少工程师？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah, our engineering team today is about 15 people.
turns.zh: 是的，我们今天工程团队大概 15 人。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: 15, yeah.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Holy moly. Okay. And then each one has five-ish Devins.
turns.zh: 我的天。好。然后每个人有五个左右 Devin。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's five times the number of Devins as engineers. What I love about this is just a glimpse into where the future is going. You guys are so ahead of how companies work with AI engineers. Seeing how you operate is going to be, as a sense, essentially how most companies will end up operating.
turns.zh: 所以 Devin 的数量是工程师的五倍。我喜欢这个的一点，就是它让人瞥见未来会去哪。你们在公司和 AI 工程师协作的方式上领先太多了。看你们怎么运作，某种意义上，基本上就是大多数公司最终会怎么运作。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah. For what it's worth, we've already seen this shift, I would say, ourselves where... In terms of the team, obviously, folks don't spend that much of their time just writing out boilerplate or just doing pure implementation of features. People get to spend much more of their time focused on really just thinking about the core questions of, "How do we make Devin better? What is the right interface for Devin? What is the right flow or the right set of features that's really going to make this as great of an experience as possible?" That's how we like things.
turns.zh: 是的。说实话，我会说我们已经看到这个转变了，我们自己——就团队而言，显然，人们不怎么把时间花在写样板代码、或者纯功能实现上。人们能把多得多的时间花在真正只思考核心问题上："我们怎么让 Devin 更好？Devin 正确的界面是什么？正确的流程、或者正确的功能集是什么，能真的让这成为尽可能好的体验？"我们喜欢那样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When is the point you reach, where there's takeoff of this being the by... Your Devin starts moving so much further ahead of everyone else. Once you have enough Devins doing all these things, they're just like wherever and you're 10 years, 20 years, 30 years, 100 years ahead.
turns.zh: 你到达那个点的时机是什么——这里开始起飞、成为……你的 Devin 开始比其他人远远领先。一旦你有足够的 Devin 做所有这些事，它们就到处都是，而你领先了 10 年、20 年、30 年、100 年。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Honestly, as a community, I think all of us as engineers around the world, I think, are going to have to think about this and build for this and adapt to these new technologies. But what I would say is, I think more and more... Especially as capabilities get better, but certainly even in studies say today, I think more and more things are going to shift towards this asynchronous flow. And one of the reasons I would say for that is in the real world, you're just capped by real world constraints. I think that one way to put it is kind of like... Don't take these numbers exactly, but it's kind of like the first order math of it is, of course, being able to write files or to complete this function or complete this line or things like that. (00:33:44): It helps a ton. It's a really great experience. There's a lot of parts of building software that obviously are almost not that at all, right? If you have a bug that you're trying to fix and so you spin up the local server, you click around on your own product on the front end and try to reproduce the bug yourself. Once you have the error, you take a look at Datadog and you see what happened and you try to find other errors in the logs. You look at those files and you see what went wrong, you make some edits, maybe you go and rerun the whole process again now that you make sure your change looks right. That's a lot of what it means to be a software engineer. These are processes that take real time. I think we're going to shift more and more towards this agentic workflow, because that's in some ways the way to really get to that 200%, 500%, 1000% gains that we'll be getting to with software engineering over the next few years.
turns.zh: 老实说，作为一个社区，我觉得我们全世界所有工程师，都得思考这个、为这个构建、适应这些新技术。但我想说的是，我觉得越来越多……尤其是随着能力变好，但肯定即使在今天的研究里，我觉得越来越多的事情会转向这种异步流程。我会说其中一个原因是，在现实世界里，你就是被现实世界的约束卡住。我觉得一种说法是 kinda 像……别精确拿这些数字，但它的一阶数学 kinda 是，当然，能写文件、或者完成这个函数、完成这一行之类的。(00:33:44)：它帮忙巨大。那是很好的体验。构建软件有很多部分显然几乎完全不是那样，对吧？如果你有个想修的 bug，你启动本地服务器，你在你自己产品的前端点来点去、试图自己复现这个 bug。一旦你有了错误，你看一眼 Datadog、看发生了什么、试图在日志里找其他错误。你看那些文件、看哪里出错了，做些修改，也许你重跑整个流程一遍、现在你确保改动看起来对了。那才是作为软件工程师很大一部分的意思。这些是需要真时间的流程。我觉得我们会越来越转向这种 agentic workflow（智能体工作流），因为那在某种意义上是真正到达未来几年我们在软件工程上会获得的 200%、500%、1000% 增益的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Enough talk. Let's show people what the heck this actually looks like. You've got a couple demos prepped that show a few use cases that you found helpful. You're going to pull up your screen and then we'll kick it off and then we'll talk as it's happening.
turns.zh: 说够了。让我们给人们看看这到底长什么样。你准备了一两个 demo，展示几个你觉得有用的用例。你要把屏幕拉起来，然后我们就启动它，然后我们边发生边聊。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah. The whole process obviously of working with Devin is working asynchronously. I thought it'd be cool for us to actually just watch Devin a little bit in action and then we can go through some other examples of work that Devin's done or things that Devin does for us, even on our team for example. But then we can check back in asynchronously with our Devin after.
turns.zh: 是的。和 Devin 一起工作的整个过程显然就是异步工作。我觉得我们实际就稍微看一会儿 Devin 在行动中会很酷，然后我们可以过一些 Devin 做过的、或者 Devin 为我们做的其他例子，比如在我们团队里。然后之后我们可以异步地再回来看我们的 Devin。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 来吧。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: I'll share this real quick. The key thing that I would just emphasize here is a lot of it obviously is really just about thinking about as a software engineer or as engineers ourselves or engineering teams, PMs, and so on. What are the things that we would want to build that we would want to hand off? We have Devin set up with our own Devin code base, for example, and so I'll go ahead and kick off with Devin for that. I'll just say, "Devin, I'm on with my friend, Lenny."
turns.zh: 我快速分享一下。我在这里要强调的关键点是，显然很大一部分真的只是关于——作为软件工程师、或者作为我们自己的工程师、或者工程团队、PM 等等——去思考我们想构建、想交出去的是什么。比如我们已经把 Devin 设置在了我们自己的 Devin 代码库上，所以我就去用 Devin 启动那个。我就说，"Devin，我在和我朋友 Lenny 连线。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hi, Devin.
turns.zh: 嗨，Devin。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: "Can you modify Devin web app two?" Let's feature your newsletter as part of the Devin website.
turns.zh: "你能改一下 Devin web app two 吗？"让我们把你的通讯作为 Devin 网站的一部分特色展示。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. On the real Devin website.
turns.zh: 来吧。在真正的 Devin 网站上。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: "Feature Lenny's site."
turns.zh: "把 Lenny 的网站特色展示出来。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, lose all your features.
turns.zh: 对，把你所有功能都丢了。

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: We're going to kick this off. As you can see, Devin gets started instantly and goes ahead and responds. Again, you can work with this asynchronously, you can work with it synchronously as well. For this, we'll just kind of go in a little bit and see exactly what's going on. But as you can see here, Devin's going through files and taking a look through a lot of stuff. We can follow here basically as we need to and see what makes sense. turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: On tasks that are well-defined. One way to put it is, you want to be giving Devin tasks, not problems. And a lot of these things like what you just saw, which was kind of like a quick front-end feature request or a bug fix or adding testing and documentation or things like that. (00:48:16): One of the things that makes a loop really nice obviously is a quick way to iterate and test. Devin will often go and log in to Devin and start a Devin session and make sure when it's working on our code base, which is kind of hilarious. But yeah, you generally want something that is kind of easy to verify and easy to test is the main thing. And you can work on bigger projects or bigger asks as well, obviously. turns.zh: 在做定义良好的任务时。一种说法是，你想给 Devin 的是任务，而不是问题。而很多这些你刚看到的，比如一个快速的前端功能请求、或者一个 bug 修复、或者加测试和文档之类的。(00:48:16)：让一个 loop 真的 nice 的一件事显然是一个快速迭代和测试的方式。所以对这种东西，显然对我们来说超级容易，比如就拉起预览、看链接工作了。显然 Devin 做也很容易。Devin 经常会去登录 Devin、启动一个 Devin 会话、确保它在我们的代码库上工作时——这有点好笑。但是的，一般来说你想要那种容易验证、容易测试的东西，这是主要的。而且你当然也能做更大的项目或更大的要求。但在那种情况下你肯定要预期需要更多地给 Devin 掌舵，确保它往正确方向走。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let me ask you this question. What's something that you guys debated a lot as you were designing and building Devin?

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: I'll give a couple that comes to mind. One I would say is a question of, I'll call it how opinionated we should be. We had the workflows that we used to Devin for, which was very much as you can see for basically integrating to our Slack and GitHub making pull requests for us in our repos, responding to issue reports or things like that. And naturally we've had certainly a lot of other different things that have come up that folks have tried. I mean, we have folks who order their DoorDash with Devin, for example. Even we have folks, certainly a lot of people who are building cool websites from scratch or working on things like that. (00:49:53): Yeah, I mean it is been an interesting trade off for us where I think the way that I would describe it is in our product, certainly the large bulk of the features that we build are for this kind of making pull requests and engineering teams use case. But I think basically our kind of general stance with all the others is obviously if folks want to use Devin for that, that's great and we want to just make sure that they're fully aware about the limitations and about where things can get caught up. (00:50:20): It is funny with AI and especially because I would say one of, I would say the most common pieces of advice out there I would say is focus on a really niche cohort. Do things that don't scale, make one use case that's really great and then you grow from there. And I think that's great advice across the board. But yeah, it's kind of interesting because I think with generative AI, you naturally see this where a lot of product experiences can turn out to be more general. And so it's an interesting trade-off for us. This is something that we still always go back and forth on and how much do we want to do more to support all the other kind of use cases out there to handle other things that folks might want to do with Devin. (00:51:03): I think another one that comes to mind is how much Devin should be, let's say a single comprehensive project experience versus a suite of tools. And as you can see here, we have Devin search, we have Devin Wiki, we have the linear ticket scooping, and certainly these tools interact with each other, but I think as time has gone on, we've seen it more and more as really building this suite of tools. And I think the core agent experience and the core kind of agent that will go off and build each of these build things for you, for example, is always of course going to be that's Devin, and that is the core piece. I think that will always be what's really special about our work. But I think that all of the other features out there, there is a complex suite of work that's required for real-world software sharing and engineering is just messy at the end of the day. (00:51:55): And so I think there are a lot of different flows and a lot of different use cases that makes sense. And an obvious thing to point out is you could ask the same questions to Devin search as you could to Devin and Devin will go through and it'll do the same thing. It'll go through and look through the files and give you an answer and stuff. (00:52:10): But with that said, on the one hand, I think on the capability side, there's certainly a lot you can do to really optimize things for very specifically question answer about this repository and that made sense to really build into a specific kind feature. (00:52:23): And then on the other side, I would say we found that users actually really, really like having this access of control. Sometimes you have a task that you're thinking about, but you actually don't want Devin to get started on the task just yet. You want to ask Devin and understand what parts of the code base might be relevant. And so you want to be very direct about saying, "This is just an ask and I just want to see the snippets of the code base that relate," or, "I just want to look at the Wiki and understand the existing representation." (00:52:50): And so it's on both the capabilities and on the UX side, we've found that that's kind of what's naturally made sense over time.
turns.zh: 我给几个浮现在脑海的。一个我会说是关于一个问题，我称之为我们应该有多"opinionated"（强主张）。我们有那些我们用来给 Devin 做的工作流，就像你基本能看到的，集成到我们的 Slack 和 GitHub、在我们的 repo 里给我们建 pull request、回应 issue 报告之类的。而且自然我们当然有很多其他人试过的不同的东西冒出来。我的意思是，我们有用 Devin 点他们 DoorDash 的人，比如。甚至我们有从零构建很酷网站、或做这类事情的人。(00:49:53)：是的，我的意思是这对我们一直是个有趣的权衡，我会描述它的方式是，在我们的产品里，当然我们建的大部分功能是为这种建 pull request、工程团队用例。但我觉得基本上我们对所有其他东西的总体立场是，显然如果人们想用 Devin 做那个，那很棒，我们只是想确保他们完全意识到那些局限、以及事情会在哪里卡住。(00:50:20)：有了 AI 这事儿很好笑，尤其是因为我会说外面最常见的建议之一是聚焦在一个真正细分的群体。做那些不规模化（do things that don't scale）的事，做一个真正很棒的用例，然后从那里成长。我觉得那是个全方位的好建议。但是的，这有点有意思，因为我觉得有了生成式 AI，你自然会看到这种——很多产品体验会变得更通用。所以对我们来说这是个有趣的权衡。这是我们仍然一直在来回纠结的事：我们想多做多少去支持外面所有那些其他用例、处理人们可能想用 Devin 做的其他事。(00:51:03)：我觉得浮现在脑海的另一个是 Devin 应该有多少……让我们说一个 si……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: Yeah, and for what it's worth, I think all of these are incredible teams. I think really smart and really forward-thinking folks who are building a lot of great products out there. And I think there's a lot to do honestly over the next few years with the advent of AGI or whatever you want to call it. I think one of the quotes that I love is in 2017, if you asked if we had AGI, the answer is no. And in 2025, if you ask if we have AGI, the answer is, "Well, you have to define AGI. And it depends on your subject." And I think it does get to the point of, I mean there is a lot of really amazing stuff happening. I think that it's easy to underrate, I would say just how big of a shift it is that we're seeing where I think there are a lot of great products out there, for example, over the last 10 years, 20 years, 30 years, that have made each of these different niches of the life cycle of building a product a little bit easier, for example, right? (00:54:28): There's great products out there for instant response, there's great products out there for logging, there's great products out there for billing, there's all of these different tools. And the obvious thing is what we're seeing with AI is all of these spaces are going to be moving multiple times faster and it's going to be like an order of magnitude shift, if anything. (00:54:47): And so I think from our perspective, we've obviously had a very specific lens that we've bet on this whole time, and that is autonomous coding agents. And there's a lot of problems to solve there, to be honest, right? There's still a ton to do on the core capabilities, certainly, and we see cases all the time where it's like, wow, why did Devin make that decision? That seems, no human engineer would've ever done that. There's all sorts of spots where, with the product interface, there's obviously a lot to think about. (00:55:16): And I think it's by the way, not just a single thing that we're working towards, but something that will change with every edition of capabilities. I kind of think of it as there's 20 generations of agent product, agent coding experiences to come. I think the one that we'll get to over the course of several years is probably something where you don't even look at the code at all, right? And you're actually just looking at your own product and you're just able to look and specify and say, "Hey, this button should be a little bit rounder. Let's do that. And by the way, let's add a new tab here and maybe we should save this information. Let's start up a database table and let's index it on X, Y, and Z columns." And you're just basically working with your products in real time and having your agent build out those things for you. Obviously there's going to be a lot of generations in between here and there, but I think the product experience itself is going to change every single time. (00:56:04): And then obviously there, there's all of the practicality of just getting it out there in the world. And so folks obviously need to learn how to use the new technology. There's a lot to do to deploy into all of the messiness of real world software. There's a lot of COBOL out there still. There's a lot of FORTRAN out there still. There's lots of kind of abstractions and details that folks have done. (00:56:27): And so I think from our perspective, we have since the beginning have been laser-focused on agentic coding, and that is the one thing that we've really believed in. It's the one thing that we've designed for and that goes all the way to even the revenue model with ACUs and having the usage-based setup. It does into obviously all the product experiences of thinking how, okay, where do you want to talk to Devin? You want to be able to talk to Devin in Slack, you want to be able to spin this up from your issue. You want to be able to all of these things and then of course the capabilities. (00:56:58): And so I don't think there's any one easy answer. I think it's obviously a combination of things, but this has been the space that we've lived in and spent all of our time in for the last year and a half, and it's going to be that way for the next five or 10 years too.
turns.zh: 是的，而且说实话，我觉得所有这些团队都不可思议。我觉得是真正聪明、真正有远见的人在构建很多很棒的产品。而且我觉得随着 AGI 或者无论你怎么叫它的到来，未来几年诚实地说有很多事要做。我喜欢的一句引语是，2017 年如果你问我们有没有 AGI，答案是没有。而 2025 年如果你问我们有没有 AGI，答案是"嗯，你得定义 AGI。而且取决于你的主体。"我觉得它确实到了那个点，我的意思是真的有很多惊人的事在发生。我觉得很容易低估——我会说我们看到的这个转变有多大，比如我觉得过去 10 年、20 年、30 年有很多很棒的产品，让构建产品生命周期的每个不同细分环节都容易了一点，比如，对吧？(00:54:28)：有做即时响应的很棒产品，有做日志的很棒产品，有做账单的很棒产品，有所有这些不同的工具。而明显的事是，我们在 AI 上看到的，是所有这些领域都会快好几倍地移动，而且如果有什么的话，那会是一个数量级的转变。(00:54:47)：所以我觉得从我们的视角，我们显然一直有一个非常具体的镜头、我们整个时间都押在上面，那就是自主编码 agent。而且老实说那里有很多问题要解决，对吧？在核心能力上当然还有一大堆要做，我们经常看到这种案例，像"哇，Devin 为什么做了那个决定？那看起来，没有任何人类工程师会那么做。"有各种地方，在产品界面上，显然有很多要思考的。(00:55:16)：而且我觉得，顺便说，我们不只是在朝一个单一的东西努力，而是某个 w……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along these lines, a big question everyone always has in AI's moats and defensibility, it's a question I've been asking every founder that comes on. How do you just think about how to build a moat in this space when it's so much easier to build and so much is built on these models that are themselves advancing so quickly?
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，一个大家总在问的大问题是 AI 的护城河和可防御性，这是我一直问每个上节目的创始人的问题。当构建变得这么容易、而且这么多是建立在这些本身飞速进步的模型上时，你怎么思考在这个领域建护城河？

turns.speaker: Scott Wu
turns.en: I'd give one slight tweak on that, which is I think it's often less about moats and more about stickiness. And what I mean by that is moats are in some sense, typically what folks mean by moats is something that means that a competitor couldn't even enter the market. And I agree that at a high level, a lot of different folks at different layers of the AI spectrum, the foundation labs or the application layer or so on, I don't think there's any kind of hard barrier that would prevent others from entering. I think what does exist is stickiness, which I would kind of define as once you have a product experience that you really like, are you excited to keep using that experience or is there an effect where it is just as easy from now on to just switch on to a new one and learn a new one and so on. (00:58:15): And I think from that perspective, I think there's a few things that are really great about coding agents in particular. One I would say is there is a lot of just inherent stickiness and learning and buildup over time, which is that as you use Devin and as your whole team uses Devin, it's the same thing with an engineer. If you're joining on day one versus you've been at the company for five years, you wrote half the code yourself, you've touched every file you've built every single piece, you know all the engineers. And so similarly, it's like Devin will really learn and build its representation of your code base and of your stack and of your process over time and will be able to do a lot more with that. (00:58:51): And then the other piece of it, which I think is really exciting I'd say is there really is a lot to do of what I would call a multiplayer aspect of code, which if you think about it, is how a lot of things get done in the real world, certainly. And so it's one thing to have your own experience, which you use yourself as just an engineer, but for example, ourselves, we see this all the time where some engineers are working with Devin and teaching Devin things and as I mentioned, folks will have Devin on board their new engineers and kind of convey that knowledge to them. (00:59:24): Or similarly, it's like I'll start a session with Devin in Slack and I'll say, "Hey, it'd be cool if we could do this thing." And some other engineer will chime in and say, "Oh, by the way, the reason we did it initially was X and Y." And so Devin, just make sure when you do this change that you still support that workflow. And Devin will say, "Okay, sounds great." Or Devin will make a PR, I'll be working with Devin, we'll make pull requests and GitHub and somebody else will be reviewing that PR or give some comments and Devin will work on that too. You'll be in linear. (00:59:52): So all these kind of spaces, it really does just kind of set up for an experience basically where Devin can just grow in the value that it can provide for your whole work over time. And so I think from that perspective, if anything, we want there to be a lot of innovation and a lot of new products and so on. I don't think that the goal is to try to lock other people out of building. There's a lot of stuff to build, and I think there's going to be a lot of different experiences. I think from our perspective, what we think about is more like how can we make Devin more and more and more useful as you're using it more?
turns.zh: 我会给那个一个小调整，就是我觉得它往往更少关于护城河、更多关于粘性（stickiness）。我的意思是，护城河在某种意义上是，通常人们说的护城河是某种意味着竞争者甚至进不了市场的东西。而且我同意在高层次上，很多在 AI 光谱不同层的人——基础实验室或者应用层等等——我不觉得有任何硬性壁垒能阻止别人进入。我觉得存在的是粘性，我会 kinda 把它定义为：一旦你有一个你真的喜欢的产品体验，你是兴奋地持续用那个体验，还是说从今往后换到一个新的、学一个新的等等，同样容易？(00:58:15)：而我觉得从那个视角，我觉得编码 agent 特别有几个真的很棒的点。一个我会说是，随着你用 Devin、随着你整个团队用 Devin，它和工程师是一回事，有大量的固有粘性和学习、以及随时间积累。也就是，随着你用 Devin，以及你整个团队用 Devin，它和工程师是一个道理。如果你第一天加入对比你在公司五年，你自己写了半个代码库、你碰过每个文件、建过每个部分、你认识所有工程师。类似地，就像 Devin 真的会学习和构建它对你代码库、对你技术栈、对你流程的表示，并随时间能用那个做多得多的事。(00:58:51)：然后另一块，我觉得真的令人兴奋，我会说是确实有很多我要称之为代码的"多人"（multiplayer）层面的事要做，如果你想想，那当然就是现实世界里很多事完成的方式。所以拥有你自己的体验、你作为工程师自己用，是一回事，但比如我们自己，我们一直看到这种，有些工程师在和 Devin 一起工作、在教……[truncated]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's very similar. turns.en: Yeah, and I think one of the things that's nice about our space too is, software engineering for better for worse has a very clear tie to value.
